Before a city wakes, it belongs to different people. Bakers move through clouds of flour. Bus drivers adjust their mirrors. Someone unlocks a corner shop and pauses with the key still warm in their hand. The streets seem less like routes than promises, waiting for footsteps to make them real.

I like the idea that ordinary life is held together by these quiet beginnings. Not grand declarations, but a kettle switched on, a chair straightened, a message answered before worry can grow. Care often arrives disguised as maintenance. It oils the hinges of the world and asks for no applause.

By noon, everything will look inevitable. The bread will simply be there. The bus will appear around the bend. We will forget how many separate acts of attention made our small conveniences possible. Perhaps gratitude begins when we interrupt that forgetting, even briefly, and notice the hands behind the day.

This is not an argument for finding beauty in everything. Some mornings are exhausting. Some work is unfairly rewarded, or not rewarded at all. Appreciation should sharpen our awareness of that imbalance, not soften it into scenery. To see someone clearly is also to wonder what they are being denied.

Still, there is hope in the daily fact of people beginning again. A shutter rises. A broom crosses a threshold. Light gathers on the windows of an early train. Nothing has been solved completely, yet breakfast is possible, and so is kindness. For now, that is somewhere solid to start.
